## Arousal as a continuously varying brain-body state

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 3
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "linear"}} }%%
flowchart TB
  A[Arousal<br/><span style='font-size:80%'>brain–body state</span>]

  A --- P[pupil diameter]
  A --- F[whisking]
  A --- L[locomotion]
  A --- H[heart rate]
  A --- N[neuromodulatory tone]
  A --- C[cortical state]
```

::: {.fragment .center}
*Arousal is inferred from proxies, not directly observed.*
:::

::: {.notes}
Arousal is a continuously varying brain-body state, and in awake mice we infer it from
several proxies: pupil diameter, whisking, locomotion, heart rate, neuromodulatory tone,
and cortical state.

The important caveat is that none of these proxies is arousal itself. Pupil diameter is
especially useful, but it is a scalar readout of a richer state.
:::

## Arousal as a continuously varying brain-body state

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Pupil = arousal proxy
- Works in quiet wakefulness
- Eye metrics track Awake/NREM/REM
- Pupil–neural coupling is state-dependent
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![McGinley *et al.*, 2015](figures/introduction/mcginley1.jpg)
:::
::::

::: footer
McGinley *et al.*, 2015; Vinck *et al.*, 2015; Turner *et al.*, 2023
:::

::: {.notes}
a. Whole-cell recording + pupil + locomotion tracking.
b. V1 L2/3 trace. Even quiet wake shows spontaneous pupil fluctuations. Dilation =
   desynchronization (suppressed 2-10 Hz). Constriction = stronger 2-10 Hz rythmic synaptic
   activity. 
c. In A1 L5 pyramidal neurons, pupil diameter tightly anticorrelates with low-frequency
   (2-10 Hz) synaptic activity.
d. Pupil diameter tightly anticorrelates with CA1 ripple cocurrence.

Take-home: pupil-linked arousal covaries with brain state even without overt movement.
:::

## Arousal changes sensory processing and behavior

![McGinley *et al.*, 2015](figures/introduction/mcginley2.jpg)

::: {.fragment .center}
*Arousal is not just a confound, it changes computation.*
:::

::: footer
McGinley *et al.*, 2015; Vinck *et al.*, 2015
:::

::: {.notes}
The previous slide showed that pupil-linked arousal covaries with brain states.

Here McGinley et al. show that these state changes matter for behavior. Mice performed
an auditory detection task while the authors tracked pupil diameter and locomotion.

During non-locomotion periods, task performance depended on pupil diameter. Hit rate
peaked at intermediate pupil diameters, and lick latency was shortest at intermediate
pupil diameters.

Small pupils, corresponding to low arousal, and large pupils, corresponding to high
arousal, were both associated with poorer performance.

Locomotion was analyzed separately. It behaved more like a high-arousal regime, with
reduced performance and increased lick latency.

The neural correlate is also important: cortical gain in auditory cortex peaked at
intermediate pupil diameter, and locomotion was associated with reduced gain.

Take-home: arousal is not just a nuisance variable. It changes sensory processing and
behavior, often nonlinearly.
:::

## Arousal can organize brain-wide dynamics

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Pupil = scalar readout
- But arousal may be a richer dynamical process
- Each readout is a different projection of that process
- These dynamics predict brain-wide physiology
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Raut *et al.*, 2025](figures/introduction/raut1.png)
:::
::::

::: footer
Stringer *et al.*, 2019; Raut *et al.*, 2025
:::

::: {.notes}
Raut et al. provide a useful conceptual bridge.

They recorded widefield calcium imaging together with face videography in awake mice.
From the video, they extracted pupil diameter and whisker motion. From imaging, they
extracted cortex-wide calcium dynamics.

The key interpretation is that all these observables are different projections of an
underlying arousal-related dynamical process.

Pupil diameter is therefore not the whole state. It is a scalar readout, or
one-dimensional projection, of a richer process evolving over time.

Their modeling uses time-delay embeddings of pupil diameter to reconstruct a latent
arousal state and predict brain-wide calcium, metabolism, and hemodynamic signals.

For our purposes, the technical details are less important than the conceptual point:
arousal can organize structured brain-wide physiology on the timescale of seconds.
:::

## Arousal-linked hemodynamics are not just bulk activity

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.incremental}
- fUSI = blood volume ≠ neural activity
- Arousal evokes brain-wide blood-volume changes
- Bulk firing misses key dynamics
:::
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
![Landemard *et al.*, 2026](figures/introduction/landemard1.png){height=450}
:::
::::

::: footer
Landemard *et al.*, 2026
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide connects the arousal story to the signal measured by fUSI.

Landemard et al. imaged blood volume with fUSI while simultaneously recording hundreds
of neurons with Neuropixels probes, mainly in visual cortex and hippocampus.

First click: they tried the standard approach. Take the average firing rate across
neurons — the bulk firing rate — and fit a hemodynamic response function to predict
blood volume. The HRF was monophasic and peaked about 1.8 seconds after neural activity,
as expected.

But this bulk model did not capture the blood-volume dynamics well. In particular,
predictions tended to lag and missed the faster changes around whisking events.

Second click: instead of averaging all neurons together, they sorted neurons by their
correlation with whisking, used as an arousal marker. Some neurons increased with
whisking: Arousal+ neurons. Others decreased with whisking: Arousal− neurons.

They then modeled blood volume as the combined contribution of these two populations,
each with its own HRF. Both HRFs were positive, but they had different timing: the
Arousal+ filter peaked earlier, around 1.2 seconds, whereas the Arousal− filter peaked
later, around 2.1 seconds, and was broader.

This combined model predicted blood volume better than the bulk firing-rate model, both
during whisking and outside whisking.

Take-home: fUSI blood-volume signals are not just average spiking activity. They can
reflect the balance between arousal-linked neural populations with different coupling to
blood volume.
:::

## Brain-wide activity is not necessarily arousal-specific

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Brain-wide recordings during visual decisions
- Action-related activity is widespread
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![Steinmetz *et al.*, 2019](figures/introduction/steinmetz1.png){height=350}
:::

::::

::: footer
Steinmetz *et al.*, 2019
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide adds an important caveat.

So far, I have been building the case that arousal can organize brain-wide physiology
and hemodynamics. But brain-wide activity is not automatically an arousal signal.

First click: Steinmetz et al. used brain-wide Neuropixels recordings during a visual
decision task. In this analysis, they fit kernels to identify which neurons carried
visual, action, or choice-related signals. The crop shown here is for the Action kernel.
The key point is that neurons whose pre-movement activity was needed to predict action
were distributed very broadly across the brain.

This means action initiation can generate brain-wide neural activity, even when that
activity is not specific to the chosen side or sensory stimulus.

Second click: they also defined an engagement index from pre-stimulus population
activity. This index was computed by projecting each trial’s pre-stimulus activity onto
the axis separating task and passive contexts.

The engagement index predicted whether the animal would make a Go response, and it
differed between Go and Miss trials across recordings. Importantly, the authors report
that this could not be fully explained by pupil diameter, overt movement, previous
reward, or inter-trial interval.

So the caution is: brain-wide signals can reflect arousal, but they can also reflect
action initiation, task engagement, or other global state variables.

This matters for the target paper because the authors need to show that the fUSI wave is
genuinely arousal-linked, and not simply a movement/action/engagement-related wave.
:::

## LC–NE: the canonical arousal system

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.incremental}
- LC sends broad noradrenergic projections
- LC stimulation rapidly dilates the pupil
- NE axons precede rapid pupil dilations
- Natural candidate for global arousal-linked hemodynamics
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![Reimer *et al.*, 2016](figures/introduction/reimer1.png)
:::
::::

::: footer
Carter *et al.*, 2010; Reimer *et al.*, 2016; Poe *et al.*, 2020
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide introduces why LC–NE is the obvious mechanistic candidate for an
arousal-linked brain-wide signal.

Reimer et al. imaged neuromodulatory axons in cortex while tracking pupil and
locomotion. The schematic shows broad cholinergic projections from basal forebrain and
noradrenergic projections from locus coeruleus to cortex.

The key point is that pupil dynamics track these neuromodulatory systems. In particular,
activity in noradrenergic axons precedes small, rapid pupil dilations during stillness.
Cholinergic axons also track pupil dilations, but somewhat less tightly for these rapid
events.

They also show causality in the LC direction: stimulation of LC, but not nearby tissue,
produces a large, rapid pupil dilation.

So, before reading the target paper, it is very natural to hypothesize that an
arousal-linked hemodynamic wave might be driven by LC–NE activity.

At the same time, this figure already hints that pupil-linked arousal is not exclusively
LC: cholinergic activity also tracks pupil dynamics, especially for broader/sustained
arousal states.
:::

## Questions of the paper

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. What is the **spatiotemporal structure** of arousal-driven hemodynamics?
2. Is it shared between **spontaneous** and **sensory-driven** arousal?
3. Is this wave dependent on **LC–NE tone**?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 5
%%| fig-height: 5
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "linear"}} }%%
flowchart LR
  S[Spontaneous arousal<br/><span style='font-size:80%'>pupil dilation</span>] --> W[Brain-wide<br/>hemodynamic wave]
  E[Sensory-driven arousal<br/><span style='font-size:80%'>evoked pupil dilation</span>] --> W

  LC[Locus coeruleus<br/>noradrenaline] -. necessary? .-> W
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This is where we enter the actual paper.

The authors are not only asking whether LC drives an arousal signal. The first question
is more descriptive and more fundamental.

Arousal is known to shape physiology, behavior, perception, and task performance. It is
also known to drive brain-wide activity, sometimes more strongly than sensory or task
variables.

But what is the structure of that effect? Is it a global increase everywhere, a
traveling wave, a region-specific sequence, or something else?

The second question is whether this structure is shared between spontaneous arousal
events and sensory-driven arousal events.

Only after establishing that there is a stereotyped arousal-linked hemodynamic wave do
they ask the mechanistic question: does this wave depend on locus coeruleus
noradrenergic tone?
:::

## Spontaneous arousal fluctuations have brain-wide fUSI correlates

![](figures/final/fig1.png)

::: {.notes}
- So to investigate relationship between spontaneous arousal fluctuations and brain-wide
  hemodynamics, the authors used fUSI on head-fixed mice within a virtual burrow assay.
- The VBA is a naturalistic behavioral setup where mice rest while simultancously
  allowing them to move back and forth during higher arousal states.
- The authors tracked pupil diameter, orofacial movements, and burrow speed as
  complementary measures of arousal.
- Brain data collection occurred through a COMBO cranial window that ranged from the
  caudal end of the olfactory bulb to the rostral edge of the cerebellum

- The arousal proxies showed strong temporal correlations with each other. Since pupil
  diameter is the most commonly used arousal proxy, they focused on it as the main proxy.
- Cross-correlation analysis between pupil diameter and fUSI signals revealed a robust,
  spatially heterogeneous brain-wide pattern of positive correlations whose strength
  varied across brain voxels.
- These correlations were strongest in cortex, thalamus and midbrain but substantial
  variability existed at finer spatial scales within these structures, indicating high
  heterogeneity both across and within anatomical units.

- To disentangle the unique contributions of each behavioral proxy, the authors employed
  partial correlation analysis. While partial correlates of all three behavioral traces
  remained present in the cortex, suggesting additive effects, only the partial
  correlates of pupil size extended into the thalamus and midbrain, closely matching the
  full correlation maps.

Take-home: spontaneous arousal fluctuations are associated with broad, structured
hemodynamic correlates.
:::

## Spontaneous arousal fluctuations have brain-wide fUSI correlates

<video controls class="hemo-video">
  <source src="figures/final/hemodynamic_wave.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

<br> 

::: {.fragment}
*Spontaneous arousal fluctuations correlate with fUSI signals across the
brain, but the pattern is spatially heterogeneous.*
:::

::: {.notes}
The key take-home from Figure 1 is not just that pupil correlates with fUSI.

The important point is that spontaneous arousal fluctuations have broad but
heterogeneous brain-wide hemodynamic correlates.

This motivates the next analysis: instead of only asking where pupil correlates with
fUSI, the authors ask whether arousal events have a stereotyped spatiotemporal
structure depending on whether they are spontaneous or sensory-driven.
:::

## Spontaneous and evoked arousal recruit shared "arousal regions"

![](figures/final/fig2.png)

::: {.notes}
- Arousal is known to increase in response to sensory stimuli, but it is unclear whether
  spontaneous and sensory-driven arousal recruit the same brain regions.
- To address this question, the authors compared the spatial patterns of fUSI
  correlations with pupil diameter during spontaneous arousal events and during
  sensory-evoked arousal events.
- Air-puff delivery was pseudo-random and associated with minimal burrow movement and
  showed no habituation across trials. Spontaneous pupil events typically occured every
  80 seconds together with burrow motion.
- Panel b shows an example recording with both spontaneous events and air-puff-evoked
  pupil responses. The important point is that the authors can compare naturally
  occurring pupil-linked arousal events with sensory-evoked pupil dilations.

- For both spontaneous and evoked arousal conditions, the authors extracted voxel-wise
  fUSI signals time-locked to arousal events. This analysis revealed a structured,
  large-scale "wave-like" propagation of hemodynamic activity from midbrain to frontal
  cortex in both conditions.
- Fiber photometry recordings in the caudal cingulate cortex, one of the common active
  areas in both waves, showed calcium activity increases across conditions, thus
  discarding a purely hemodynamic explanation of these responses.
- Other controls where done (white noise instead of air puffs, air puffs under
  anesthesia) to rule out the possibility that the wave was driven by sensory input or
  movement.

- The authors found that a large fraction (67.9%) of brain regions significantly active
  during either spontaneous or evoked arousal overlapped across both conditions. These
  core arousal regions comprised most of the thalamus as well as large portions of the
  midbrain and cortex.

Take-home: spontaneous and sensory-driven arousal recruit overlapping fUSI-defined
arousal regions. This answers the generality question at the regional level, but not yet
at the level of temporal dynamics.
:::

## Arousal propagates from brainstem to cortex

![](figures/final/fig3.png)

::: {.notes}
- Figure 2 showed that spontaneous and evoked arousal recruit overlapping brain regions.
  Figure 3 asks whether the temporal structure of the response is also shared.

- Panel a maps the time-to-peak of the fUSI response across coronal slices, separately
  for spontaneous pupil events and air puffs. While spontancous arousal spanned over a
  longer timeframe than evoked arousal (5.70 vs. 4.37 seconds, respectively), the
  spatial organization of the delay maps was remarkably conserved, with cortical regions
  consistently peaking later than subcortical regions in both conditions.
- The key visual result is a temporal gradient: the response peaks earlier in brainstem
  and subcortical regions, and later in cortical regions.

- To facilitate comparisons, the authors grouped the voxel-wise delays into anatomical
  regions belonging to the core arousal network. The region-wise relative delays were
  highly correlated across spontaneous and evoked conditions, confirming a common
  activation sequence that originated in the midbrain and propagated frontally and
  laterally along the cortex

- To assess whether the observed timing differences reflected neural population dynamics
  rather than region-specific hemodynamic coupling, the authors leveraged an independent
  fiber photometry dataset acquired in awake mice within the VBA. Fiber photometry
  recordings showed calcium activity increases around pupil events, with region-specific
  fiber photometry delays between calcium signal and pupil peak dilation closely
  matching the fUSI-derived times until maximum activation

Take-home: the shared arousal response is not just a set of overlapping regions. It has
a consistent spatiotemporal structure, with a brainstem-to-cortex temporal gradient, and
this sequence is shared between spontaneous and sensory-driven arousal.
:::

## PCA captures the shared arousal wave

![](figures/final/fig4.png)

::: {.notes}
- Figure 3 showed the arousal response as a temporal gradient across regions, from
  brainstem to cortex.
- Figure 4 asks whether this shared wave can be captured in a lower-dimensional
  representation of the fUSI signal.
- Indeed, low-dimensional representations of brain activity in selected regions often
  reflect behavioral proxies of arousal (Stringer *et al.*, 2019; Raut *et al.*, 2025).

- Panel a shows the group PCA approach. They compute session-level covariance matrices
  from stimulus-free recordings, average them, and decompose this group covariance
  matrix to obtain spatial principal components. Then they project new fUSI sessions,
  including both spontaneous recordings and air-puff sessions, onto these components to
  get temporal weights.
- They regressed the global signal out before performing PCA.
- They retained the first 2 PCs, which together explained around 65% of the variance.
- PC1 was cortex dominated, while PC2 was thamalic- and midbrain-dominated. Both PCs are
  highly correlated with pupil size, and PC2 temporally preceded PC1, consistent with
  the brainstem-to-cortex gradient observed in Figure 3.

- To test generalization, they projected the held-out spontaneous *and* evoked sessions
  onto the PCs and found that these components reconstructed a comparable fraction of
  variance at the response peak in both cases (~30%), consistent with a shared latent
  structure underlying both conditions.
- The PCs also captured the timescale differences between conditions, with broader
  responses during spontaneous arousal and sharper responses  during evoked arousal.

- Panel g shows the resulting trajectory in PCA space. Spontaneous and evoked arousal
  follow similar low-dimensional trajectories.

Take-home: the arousal-linked hemodynamic wave can be summarized as a shared
low-dimensional trajectory that is both recoverable from spontaneous activity and
predictive of fUSI and pupillary repsonses across spontaneous and evoked arousal
conditions. This is consistent with the view that both spontaneous and evoked responses
reflect a common arousal state.
:::

## LC–NE manipulations change global perfusion

![](figures/final/fig5.png)

::: {.notes}
- Figure 5 starts the mechanistic part of the paper.
- Until now, the authors have established that spontaneous and evoked arousal recruit
  overlapping fUSI regions and follow a shared brainstem-to-cortex temporal gradient.

- The association between arousal state and the LC-NE system is well-established, with
  LC activity increasing in response to both spontaneous and evoked arousal.
- However, while tonic LC activations have been shown to broadly modulate brain-wide
  signals, the causal relationship between LC activity  and arousal-dependent brain-wide
  dynamics has not yet been established.
- So now they ask whether LC noradrenergic tone is necessary for these hemodynamic
  dynamics.

- For this purpose, they used optogenetics to manipulate LC activity while recording
  fUSI in the VBA. Opsins targeted to noradrenergic neurons were expressed in the LC,
  and optic fibers were implanted to allow for optogenetic stimulation or inhibition of
  LC activity. One important detail is that the fUSI field of view is shorter because of
  the optic fiber placement.
- Compared to the control, LC optogenetic activation produced immediate and significant
  pupil dilation that persisted throughout stimulation and rapidly returned to baseline
  afterwards. 

- By contrast, sustained LC optogenetic silencing caused a delayed shift towards pupil
  constriction that however did not reach statistical significance, likely due to a
  physiological floor effect. At the whole-brain level, neither manipulation elicited
  the previously identified arousal wave.
- Rather, optogenetic stimulation induced sign-consistent shifts in fUSI baseline signal
  during the entire duration of the manipulation period, namely decreases during LC
  activation and increases during LC inhibition. These fUSI signal shifts were
  widespread and spatially structured, but different from the spatiotemporal
  organization of the arousal wave.

Take home: LC manipulation is not weak or ineffective. Sustained manipulation of
noradrenergic tone clearly changes brain perfusion. This is important because the next
question is sharper: even though LC–NE tone changes perfusion, does it actually
determine the arousal-linked wave structure?
:::

## LC–NE tone is not required for the arousal wave

![](figures/final/fig6.png)

::: {.notes}
- First, the authors noticed that although reduced in magnitude, spontaneous pupil
  events continued to occur during sustained LC activation and inhibition, together with
  fUSI responses whose spatial structure paralleled those of the arousal wave in control
  animals.

- Panel b and e show normalized brain-wide fUSI response amplitude for spontaneous and
  evoked pupil events during concurrent optogenetic manipulation, across the control, LC
  activation, and LC inhibition cohorts. The regional response structure is largely
  preserved.

- Panel c and f compare regional response amplitudes between controls and either ChR2
  activation or ACR2 inhibition. If LC tone were necessary for the arousal wave, we
  might expect strong disruption or loss of correspondence with controls.

- In a complementary analysis, the authors examined the correlation maps between fUSI
  signals and face motion, another arousal proxy that is not influenced by the
  optostimulation itself, unlike pupil size. Correlation maps remained stable across
  cohorts both during and outside optostimulation periods, likewise indicating a lack of
  effect of LC manipulations over spontaneous arousal correlates.

Take home: even though LC–NE manipulations affect global perfusion, they do not abolish
or strongly impair the spatial structure of the arousal-linked fUSI response. LC
noradrenergic tone modulates brain perfusion, but the arousal wave itself persists
during both LC activation and inhibition.
:::

## Main take-home

<br>

*Arousal is not a uniform global signal.*

<br>

::: {.incremental}
- Spontaneous and evoked arousal recruit overlapping fUSI regions
- Both conditions follow a **subcortex-to-cortex temporal gradient**
- The wave is captured by a low-dimensional fUSI subspace
- LC–NE tone changes perfusion, but does **not** abolish the wave
:::

::: {.notes}
The paper does not simply show that arousal increases brain-wide fUSI signal. Instead,
it shows that arousal has a structured spatiotemporal organization.

Spontaneous pupil events and sensory-evoked arousal recruit overlapping regions, and
these responses follow a consistent temporal sequence from subcortical regions toward
cortex.

The PCA analysis shows that this wave is not only visible in event averages. It is also
embedded in ongoing resting-state fUSI activity as a low-dimensional structure.

Finally, LC manipulations strongly affect vascular signal amplitude, so they are not
ineffective. But they do not abolish the arousal-linked wave.

So the take-home is: arousal evokes a stereotyped brain-wide hemodynamic wave, but this
wave is not simply tonic LC–NE tone.
:::

## Interpretation

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### What the wave may reflect
::: {.incremental}
- a generalized arousal state
- bottom-up subcortical → cortical recruitment
- shared latent dynamics across spontaneous and sensory-driven arousal
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### What LC–NE may do
::: {.incremental}
- modulates vascular/perfusion baseline
- contributes to arousal physiology
- not sufficient to reproduce the full wave
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
*LC–NE modulates the system, but may not generate the arousal wave.*
:::

::: {.notes}
This is how I would interpret the paper.

The authors propose that spontaneous and evoked arousal share a common latent structure.
This fits with the idea of generalized arousal: different triggers can bring the animal
into a similar brain-body state.

The subcortex-to-cortex sequence suggests that arousal is not just a synchronous global
gain change. It unfolds over time.

The LC result is subtle. LC is still relevant to arousal. The optogenetic manipulation
changed pupil and global perfusion, so noradrenaline clearly affects brain and body
state.

But sustained LC activation or inhibition did not reproduce the wave, and did not
prevent the wave during spontaneous or evoked arousal.

So a careful conclusion is: tonic LC–NE tone is not the primary driver of this fUSI
arousal wave. Other systems, especially acetylcholine, or interactions among multiple
neuromodulators, may be more important.
:::

## Caveats

::: {.incremental}
- **fUSI is hemodynamic**: blood volume is an indirect proxy for neural activity.
- **Movement is intertwined with arousal**: controlled, but residual motor contributions
  cannot be excluded.
- **LC manipulation was tonic**: phasic LC activity or projection-specific LC effects
  may still matter.
- **Optogenetics may affect neurovascular coupling**: especially because noradrenaline
  can act on vascular tone.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide for journal club discussion.

First, fUSI measures blood volume, not neural activity directly. The authors support a
neural interpretation using prior fUSI literature and fiber photometry controls, but the
signal remains hemodynamic.

Second, movement and arousal are tightly coupled. The authors use mild air puffs,
partial correlations, light-driven pupil controls, and anesthesia controls, but residual
motor contributions cannot be completely ruled out.

Third, the LC manipulation is sustained and tonic. The result argues against tonic
noradrenergic tone as the primary driver, but it does not rule out phasic LC
contributions, projection-specific LC effects, or incomplete inhibition.

Fourth, because noradrenaline affects vascular tone, LC optogenetic manipulation might
alter neurovascular coupling itself.

Finally, the wave’s causal generator is still open. The authors point toward other
neuromodulatory mechanisms, especially acetylcholine, but the circuit mechanism remains
a natural next question.
:::

## Conclusion

<br><br><br>

::: {.center}
*Arousal engages a heterogenous, brain-wide hemodynamic wave independent of
noradrenergic tone.*
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the final one-sentence conclusion.

Arousal is not just a global scalar or a confound to regress out. In this paper, it
appears as a reproducible brain-wide dynamical motif.

The open question is what circuit mechanism generates this motif if tonic LC
noradrenergic tone is not sufficient or necessary.
:::
